title: Welsh NHS targeted intervention: Betsi Cadwaladr's decade of crisis
narrative_md:
**Wales's largest health board has spent nine of the last ten years under some form of special measures. It is about to start a tenth.**

On 27 June 2024, Welsh Health Secretary Eluned Morgan placed Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board back into 'targeted intervention' — the highest level of escalation in the Welsh NHS framework. The board, created in 2009 from the merger of three predecessor organisations, has now been in some form of enhanced oversight for all but 32 months of its existence.

Betsi Cadwaladr covers all of North Wales — 700,000 people, three acute hospitals (Ysbyty Glan Clwyd, Ysbyty Gwynedd, Wrexham Maelor), and a workforce of 19,000. It was formed by the 2009 Welsh NHS restructure that abolished trusts and combined commissioning and provider functions into seven health boards. Size was the point: critics warned at the time that a single board covering the entire north of Wales would be ungovernable. They were right.

The first escalation came in June 2015, when the then-Labour Welsh Government placed the board in special measures over governance, leadership and maternity failings at the Tawel Fan ward in Ysbyty Glan Clwyd. It stayed in special measures until November 2020 — five and a half years, the longest intervention in UK NHS history. De-escalation lasted 28 months. In February 2023 it was re-escalated over the same issues: governance instability, financial deterioration, mental-health service failures, and a revolving door of chief executives.

June 2024's targeted intervention is the formal mid-tier between 'routine monitoring' and 'special measures.' The triggers were a £56 million deficit in 2023-24 (against a £2.0 billion turnover), the failure to meet planned-care recovery targets, and a fresh Royal College of Nursing report on maternity safety. The board's chief executive Carol Shillabeer, appointed in 2023, retained her post but lost operational autonomy over finance and planning.

The financial picture is bleak. The Welsh NHS budget for 2024-25 is £11.5 billion, of which Betsi Cadwaladr takes £2.0 billion. A £56 million deficit is 2.8% of turnover — survivable in isolation, but recurring. Four of Wales's seven health boards were in deficit in 2023-24; total Welsh NHS overspend was £354 million, absorbed by the Welsh Government from reserves that are now essentially empty.

The clinical picture is bleaker. Waiting list data for December 2024 showed Wales with the worst elective-care performance of the four UK nations: 22% of patients waiting over a year, against 5% in England. Betsi Cadwaladr was below the Welsh average on six of ten NHS Wales performance indicators.

Structural reform is politically difficult. Breaking up Betsi Cadwaladr would require abolishing a 15-year-old board in the run-up to the 2026 Senedd election. Morgan has instead commissioned an independent review — the third since 2013 — reporting in mid-2026.

The Welsh NHS story is a warning about devolution without redesign. When Wales gained responsibility for health in 1999, it inherited an NHS structure copied from England. Subsequent structural changes have diverged — but without the financial or workforce headroom to absorb the disruption. Betsi Cadwaladr is the most visible symptom.
